03.event: Missing the study hall, Rabbi Eliezer met Rabbi Asi and asked what had been taught there.
03.turn: Told the law follows Rabbi Yosei, he inferred that only a single authority disagrees.
03.outcome: The exchange moves into legal argument; Rabbi Asi's answer comes in the following segment.
03.summary: Rabbi Eliezer did not attend the study hall, so he met Rabbi Asi, who was standing, and asked what had been said. Rabbi Asi reported that Rabbi Yohanan ruled like Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Eliezer asked whether this implies a lone dissenter, and Rabbi Asi answered yes, citing a baraita.
03.missing: There is little event beyond a chance meeting and a legal exchange; no real turn or resolution.

04.event: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov was struck by suskhinta, the illness caused by holding back from urinating during Rav Huna's long lectures, and was hung from the cedar pillar of the study hall.
04.turn: A green substance came out of him and he was cured.
04.outcome: He said that of sixty elders who all became impotent from Rav Huna's discourse, he alone escaped, by wisdom preserving its owner.
04.summary: Several sages, including Rav Giddel, Rav Helbo and Rav Sheshet, became impotent from holding back during Rav Huna's lectures. Rav Aha bar Ya'akov fell ill with the same condition, was hung from the cedar pillar of the study hall, and a green substance emerged, healing him. He later said that of sixty elders only he escaped, since wisdom preserves its possessor.

05.event: Sitting among Rome's nobles in a gold cloak, Dama was approached by his mother, who tore the cloak off, hit him on the head and spat in his face.
05.turn: He was publicly humiliated by his own mother.
05.outcome: He did not shame her in return.
05.summary: Dama ben Netina once sat among the nobles of Rome wearing a fine gold cloak. His mother came, tore the garment from him, smacked his head and spat in his face. He did not embarrass her.

06.actor: The household of the prince and the judges Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha and Rabbi Abba
06.event: The prince's household seized an orphans' maidservant for a debt, and the judges approved the seizure.
06.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of currying favor and noted that Reish Lakish had earlier reversed a judgment made under Rabbi Tarfon's rule.
06.outcome: Not stated within the passage; only an objection is left standing.
06.summary: The prince's household seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley to collect a debt. Judges including Rabbi Abbahu approved it as well done. Rabbi Abba objected that they were flattering the household, since Reish Lakish had overturned a similar ruling.
06.missing: What the judges did after Rabbi Abba's objection; the case's final result.

07.actor: A fox and the people who weighed the turnip
07.event: A fox nested in a turnip, and the turnip was weighed.
07.turn: Even without the hollowed space it weighed sixty litra.
07.outcome: Offered as proof that giant future wheat is not implausible.
07.summary: A fox once made its nest inside a turnip. People weighed the turnip and found, even discounting the dug-out space, that it weighed sixty litra by the Tzippori measure. This is cited to show that wheat as large as ox kidneys is not far-fetched.
07.missing: The fox incident is a one-line proof within a homiletic prediction; no actors, setting or resolution are given.

08.event: Rav Safra challenged Rava that the Tigris separates Akistefon and Ardeshir by more than 141 and a third cubits, yet they are treated as one city.
08.turn: Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the Tigris about seventy cubits away.
08.outcome: The challenge was answered, because the cities are linked by the submerged wall.
08.summary: Rav Safra pointed out to Rava that the Tigris separates Akistefon and Ardeshir by more than the allowed distance, yet they are measured as a single city. Rava went out and showed him the foundations of a wall submerged in the river at seventy cubits and a remainder. That linked the two cities and answered the objection.

09.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman, who noticed from her voice that she was from Mehoza.
09.turn: He first ruled by the Babylonian custom, but when told she married into Neharde'a he reversed to the Neharde'a custom.
09.outcome: He ruled that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel, extending as far as the Neharde'a kav measure is used.
09.summary: A woman of Mehoza who had married into Neharde'a came with her husband before Rav Nahman. Hearing her accent, he said Babylonia follows Rav. When told she was married to a Neharde'a man, he said that Neharde'a and its towns follow Shmuel, and defined Neharde'a's boundary by its measures.

11.actor: Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Yishmael, Rav Shemen bar Abba
11.event: Rav Dimi and Ravin reported that a case about a wife's sustenance came before Rabbi in Beit She'arim and Rabbi Yishmael in Tzippori, with opposite rulings.
11.turn: Rabbi Yohanan questioned why one sage refused sustenance, and Rav Shemen bar Abba said Shmuel had already explained it as a case where the husband was heard to be dead.
11.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan responded in astonishment, 'Have you gone that far?'
11.summary: Rav Dimi reported that one case of a wife's sustenance came before Rabbi and another before Rabbi Yishmael, and they ruled in opposite ways. Rabbi Yohanan was puzzled by the one who refused it, and Rav Shemen bar Abba said Shmuel in Babylonia had explained it as a case where the husband was reported dead. Rabbi Yohanan answered in astonishment. Ravin's version swaps which judge ruled which way.
11.missing: The cases' facts and final outcomes are not given; the passage is mostly a legal discussion framed by reports.

12.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
12.event: She came before Rav Yosef asking him to set her sustenance, then wine, then silk garments.
12.turn: When he asked why she needed silk, she replied it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends.
12.outcome: Her quip ends the account; whether silk was granted is not stated.
12.summary: A widow, the wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya, came before Rav Yosef and asked for sustenance and wine, which he granted. She then asked for silk, and when he asked why, she said it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends, so she would not be ashamed in front of them.
12.missing: Whether Rav Yosef granted the silk.

13.actor: Rabba bar bar Hanna and Abaye
13.event: Rabba bar bar Hanna said he saw an Arab cut open his camel, which died before it could stop braying.
13.turn: Abaye answered that the camel was emaciated and so died instantly.
13.outcome: Abaye's answer neutralized the objection to the earlier ruling.
13.summary: Rabba bar bar Hanna said he personally saw an Arab slash open his camel with a sword, and it died before its braying stopped. Abaye said that camel was emaciated and weak, so a normal one would not die so quickly.
13.missing: The anecdote is a brief eyewitness proof inside a legal argument; no real story arc.

14.actor: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa and Rav Ashi
14.event: Each stood as waiter before a master (Mar Shmuel, Rav Kahana) when a strongly aromatic dish was brought.
14.turn: Without a share they said they would have been endangered by the craving.
14.outcome: The Gemara draws a general rule that anything fragrant or sharp-tasting should be offered to the waiter.
14.summary: Rav Anan bar Tahalifa recalled standing before Mar Shmuel as a mushroom dish was served and said he would have been endangered had he not been given some. Rav Ashi told a similar story about turnip slices in vinegar before Rav Kahana. The Gemara concludes that anything aromatic or sharp must be shared with the waiter.
14.missing: These are brief first-person testimonies for a rule; no developed plot.

15.event: When people sought to make Babylonian lineage the muddled one, Rabbi Pinehas told his servants to carry him off on a stretcher after he spoke two statements in the study hall.
15.turn: After a decoy ruling he said the lineage statement that Eretz Yisrael is muddled relative to Babylonia, and his servants fled with him.
15.outcome: Those pursuing could not catch him; they investigated families until they reached powerful ones, found it dangerous and withdrew.
15.summary: When some sought to cast Babylonian lineage as inferior, Rabbi Pinehas arranged for his servants to carry him away on a stretcher once he had spoken. In the study hall he first stated a decoy ruling, then declared that Eretz Yisrael is muddled relative to Babylonia, and was whisked away. The scholars chased him in vain, then examined families until they reached powerful ones and backed off.

16.event: On his deathbed Rabbi named Babylonian places and the sins or flawed lineage of their inhabitants, including a town whose people trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them.
16.turn: He moved from condemnation to naming Adda bar Ahava of Akra DeAgma.
16.outcome: The statement is cut off; the following segment finishes it (Adda bar Ahava is in Abraham's lap, Rav Yehuda was born).
16.summary: As Rabbi lay dying, he said which Babylonian towns were tainted, such as Homanya's Ammonites and Masgariya's mamzerim. He told of Bireta DeSatya, where people trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after being excommunicated. He then mentioned Adda bar Ahava of Akra DeAgma, who that day sits in Abraham's lap, and said Rav Yehuda was born.
16.missing: The end of the deathbed statement is in segment [5]; much of it is a list of places rather than a plotted event.

17.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify, but Rav Ashi at first did not remember, and Rav Kahana jogged his memory.
17.turn: Rav Ashi ultimately remembered and testified, then saw Rav Kahana hesitant to accept it.
17.outcome: Rav Ashi told him he was not relying on Rav Kahana's prompting but had made the effort himself to remember.
17.summary: Rav Ashi knew testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. Rav Kahana asked if he remembered, and Rav Ashi said no, then Rav Kahana described the incident. Eventually Rav Ashi remembered and testified, and seeing Rav Kahana hesitant he said he had not relied on him but had strained himself to recall.

18.event: Ten men carried a woman out on a bier as if she were dead and had intercourse with her.
18.turn: This showed that immoral men are not restrained by being many.
18.outcome: Rav Yosef used it to argue that ten men will join in wrongdoing without shame, as ten will steal a beam together.
18.summary: Once ten men carried a woman out on a bier as though she were dead and abused her. Rav Yosef cited this, with the example of ten people jointly stealing a beam, to show a group of immoral men feel no shame before each other.
18.missing: Only a one-line incident, with no names or details, used to support a ruling.

19.event: On his deathbed Rabbi named Babylonian places and the sins or lineage problems of their inhabitants, including a town that trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized.
19.turn: He ended by saying that today Adda bar Ahava sits in Abraham's lap and that Rav Yehuda was born.
19.outcome: The statement ends with Rav Yehuda's birth; the later commentary on the chain of righteous people is not part of the story.
19.summary: As Rabbi lay dying, he listed Babylonian towns with tainted populations, including Bireta DeSatya, whose people trapped fish on Shabbat and apostatized after being excommunicated. He then said Adda bar Ahava, just circumcised, sits in Abraham's lap, and announced that Rav Yehuda was born that day.
19.missing: Mostly a list of places; the deathbed utterance has a context but little plot.

20.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
20.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with a cheap covering on his head, hurrying a child to the synagogue, and asked what the fuss was.
20.turn: Rabbi Yehoshua answered by citing the verse linking teaching one's children to standing at Horeb.
20.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba then refused to eat before teaching a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna did likewise.
20.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue with a cloth thrown over his head. Asked why, Rabbi Yehoshua said that the Torah links teaching one's children to standing at Mount Sinai. From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat until he had taught a child, and Rabba bar Rav Huna would not eat before bringing a child to the study hall.
